text: Great video, Prateek and team. The only thing I’ll say about SIPs as a 38-year-old is that while what you said is correct - inflation should be accounted for while setting a long-term financial goal in mind - it’s equally important from a discipline standpoint. In my 20s, had someone told me that this accumulates and compounds, it’s likely I would have put a percentage of my take-home into an SIP as savings instead of routing it all into consumption. While I only started SIPs much later, at 32, I do see the benefits of putting aside the 40k-odd every month that I do now. It’s not likely to compound into a massive amount of money but a decent cumulative XIRR of 12-13% over the years should give me at least a decent nest egg for retirement. What I’ve actually benefited more from is the discipline of saving, which should be something that someone in their 20s on a regular salary should consider early, whatever the amount.

SIPs have an inherent flaw as there is no intelligence involved & the averaging math doesn’t help. So, that’s the reason you see most equity MFs failed to generate good returns even in past 5 yrs.

text:
When Direct plans were first introduced I had followed this approach:
 Stop my SIPs in the regular plans.
 Start the same SIPs in the Direct Funds
 STP from Regular Plan to Direct Plan keeping the Exit Loads & LTGC in mind. That is, if I had a SIP active till last month, I create a STP such that the last STP transactions happens 12 months after the last SIP in the regular Plan so that I cross the 1 year period - both for Exit Load and LTGC - for each SIP transactions.
 This last point is important - each SIP is actually a “Purchase” in the MF and will incur Exit Load and LTGC rules accordingly. I designed a “rolling pull out” so that each SIP date was taken care of. By this means I managed not t pay any Exit Load or STGC for my investments in the Regular Plans.
 Also, the agent cannot deduct anything from your account. You don’t have to depend on them at all. Just use the Folio Number to start a STP or redemption as the case might be. This can be done directly on the AMC’s web site after eKYC and account creation. And you don’t need the agent’s permission to make changes to your investments - they are your and you have total control over them. The agent does not.

text:
Hello Team,
 I’d like to suggest an enhancement to the SIP functionality that would give investors more flexibility and ease of use.
 Use Case: 
SIPs are executed automatically on their scheduled date, as they should (e.g., the 28th of each month). However, there are scenarios where I may see a market opportunity and prefer to execute my SIP earlier; for example, on August 14th instead of waiting until the 28th.
 Proposed Feature: 
 Add an “Execute Now” option for the SIP.
 While executing early, provide a checkbox/option to skip the upcoming scheduled execution (to avoid double execution for the same month).
 Extended Request (Bulk Actions): 
 A bulk option to apply “Execute Now” or “Skip This Month” across multiple SIPs at once.
 Similarly, a bulk reschedule option to adjust SIP dates, rather than editing them one by one.
 Current Workaround: 
Right now, the only way to handle this is by editing each SIP and backdating it so it won’t trigger again this month, then placing my order manually, which is quite time-consuming.
 This feature would make SIP investing more convenient, especially for investors managing multiple SIPs.
 Thanks for considering this!
context: Feature Request - Coin: Flexible SIP Execution & Skip Option (+ Bulk Actions)
